Put \(G_0=\prod_{g\in\mathcal G}\mathfrak S_{s_g}\), with the uniform law on this finite group.  For \(\gamma=(\gamma_g)_g\in G_0\), write \(\gamma x\) for the assignment obtained by replacing every subset \(S_g\) by \(\gamma_gS_g\), and define
\[
 (\gamma y)_{gi}(z,a)=y_{g,\gamma_g^{-1}(i)}(z,a).
\]
The condition in \(\texttt{ass:stratified-interference}\) makes this a well-defined action on complete schedules and on revealed vectors.  The coordinate bounds and the anonymous-saturation property in \(\texttt{def:model-class}\) are invariant under the action.  Also, because the estimand averages with the same coefficient \(c_{z,a}\) over all units,
\[
 \tau(\gamma y)=\tau(y).                                                    \tag{1}
\]

Draw \(X_0\sim D\) and \(\gamma\) uniformly and independently, and set \(X'=\gamma X_0\).  Let \(\widetilde D\) be the law of \(X'\).  Conditional on \(X'=x\), randomize the old rule by
\[
 Z_x(v,\gamma)=\delta(\gamma^{-1}x,\gamma^{-1}v),
\]
where the conditional law of \(\gamma\) is the one induced by \((X_0,\gamma)\) given \(X'=x\).  This law depends on \(D\) and \(x\), but not on the unknown schedule.  Hence
\[
 \widetilde\delta(x,v)
   =\mathbb E[Z_x(v,\gamma)\mid X'=x]                                      \tag{2}
\]
is a genuine measurable rule based only on \((x,v)\), and it remains in \([-L,L]\) by convexity of that interval.
On an assignment with \(\widetilde D(x)=0\), define \(\widetilde\delta(x,v)=0\); this totalizes the rule without changing its risk.

Fix \(y\in\mathcal M\).  Conditional Jensen applied to (2), followed by (1), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R(\widetilde D,\widetilde\delta;y)
 &\le {1\over |G_0|}\sum_{\gamma\in G_0}
     \mathbb E_D\!\left[
       \{\delta(X_0,(\gamma^{-1}y)|_{\mathcal O(X_0)})
           -\tau(\gamma^{-1}y)\}^2\right]  \\
 &={1\over |G_0|}\sum_{\gamma\in G_0}
       \mathcal R(D,\delta;\gamma^{-1}y)
 \le \sup_{y'\in\mathcal M}\mathcal R(D,\delta;y').
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{3}
\]
Every step in (3) uses only the group invariance just established and Jensen's inequality for the convex function \(u\mapsto u^2\).

It remains to identify the new assignment law.  Unit permutations do not change the label vector.  Fix a label vector \(a=(a_g)_g\) and arbitrary original subsets \((S_g^0)_g\) having the prescribed sizes.  Since the \(\gamma_g\)'s are independent and uniform,
\[
 \Pr\{\gamma_gS_g^0=T_g\text{ for every }g\mid A=a,(S_g^0)_g\}
   =\prod_{g\in\mathcal G}{1\over\binom{s_g}{r_{s_g,a_g}}}                 \tag{4}
\]
for every feasible \((T_g)_g\).  The right side of (4) is independent of the original subsets, so averaging their possibly dependent conditional law leaves the same product.  Thus, under \(\widetilde D\), the subsets are independent and uniform conditional on the complete label vector, while the original arbitrary joint label law is unchanged.  Formula (4) is also valid at \(r_{q,a}=0\) or \(q\), because the corresponding binomial coefficient is one; it uses neither saturation variation nor interior counts.

The class of conditionally uniform pairs is contained in the unrestricted class, whereas (3) maps every unrestricted pair to a conditionally uniform pair with no larger worst-case risk.  Taking the two infima proves that imposing conditional uniformity leaves \(R^\star\) unchanged.

We divide the proof into endpoint completion, symmetry reduction, construction of the orbit kernel, and minimax duality.

First, \(\sum_{z,a}c_{z,a}=0\) implies
\[
 \sum_{z,a:c_{z,a}>0}c_{z,a}
 =-\sum_{z,a:c_{z,a}<0}c_{z,a}
 ={1\over2}\sum_{z,a}|c_{z,a}|=L.
\]
Together with \(0\le Y_{gi}(z,a)\le1\) from \(\texttt{ass:bounded-outcomes}\), this proves \(|\tau(Y)|\le L\), so clipping an estimator to \([-L,L]\) cannot increase squared error.

Fix a design \(D\) and an endpoint table \(d\).  For a complete \(y\in\mathcal M\), independently draw every coordinate
\[
 B_{gi}(z,a)\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(y_{gi}(z,a)).                       \tag{5}
\]
The restriction of (5) to \(\mathcal O(x)\) is exactly the conditional Bernoulli experiment in \(\texttt{def:endpoint-extension}\).  Linearity of \(\tau\) gives \(\mathbb E_B\tau(B)=\tau(y)\).  Therefore, for every assignment \(x\),
\[
 \overline d(x,y|_{\mathcal O(x)})-\tau(y)
 =\mathbb E_B\!\left[d(x,B|_{\mathcal O(x)})-\tau(B)\right].             \tag{6}
\]
Jensen's inequality in (6), followed by expectation over \(X\sim D\), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R(D,\overline d;y)
 &\le \mathbb E_B\mathcal R(D,d;B)\\
 &\le \max_{b_0\in\mathcal M\cap\{0,1\}^{2KN}}
            \mathcal R(D,d;b_0).
\end{aligned}                                                               \tag{7}
\]
This proves the displayed extension inequality.  Restricting nature from the cube to its vertices gives the reverse minimax inequality.  Taking the infimum over endpoint tables in (7) consequently proves endpoint equivalence, first for every fixed \(D\), and then after minimizing over \(D\).  The finite endpoint decision cube is compact, so the endpoint minimizer is attained.

Now enlarge the group in the preceding lemma to \(\Gamma\), also allowing permutations of equal-size clusters.  The model cube, assignment set, observation relation, and scalar target are invariant.  Repeating the averaging and conditional-Jensen calculation of \(\texttt{lem:conditional-uniformity}\) shows that an invariant procedure is no worse in maximum risk.  If \(B(\Pi)\) denotes the minimum Bayes risk under a prior \(\Pi\) on binary schedules, then \(B\) is concave, because it is an infimum of functions linear in \(\Pi\).  Hence
\[
 B\!\left({1\over|\Gamma|}\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\gamma\Pi\right)
 \ge {1\over|\Gamma|}\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}B(\gamma\Pi)=B(\Pi).       \tag{8}
\]
Thus both players may be restricted to invariant strategies.

Let \(h_0=2^{2K}\).  A binary unit response is one of \(h_0\) complete \(2K\)-bit vectors.  Consequently a size-\(q\) cluster response type is a multiset of \(q\) such vectors, and their number is
\[
 B_q=\binom{q+h_0-1}{h_0-1}=\binom{q+h_0-1}{q}.                             \tag{9}
\]
An invariant global response is the size-tagged histogram \(\kappa\) of these cluster types.  An invariant assignment is the histogram \(n=(n_{q,a})\).  Conditional uniformity shows that, given \(n\), labels are allocated uniformly among equal-size clusters and the treated subsets are then independent and uniform.  For label \(a\), a local binary observation is the triple \((a,u,v)\), with
\[
 0\le u\le r_{q,a},\; 0\le v\le q-r_{q,a};                               \tag{10}
\]
there are \(O_q=\sum_a(r_{q,a}+1)(q-r_{q,a}+1)\) such triples.  Notice that the response type in (9) retains the joint \(2K\)-bit vector of each unit; no pairwise-conflict or marginal-total replacement has been made.

For a fixed cluster response type \(t\), direct counting under uniform exact-count sampling gives precisely the rational probability \(P_{t,a}(u,v)\) in \(\texttt{def:local-kernel}\).  Expanding
\[
 F_{\kappa,q}(z)=\prod_t
 \left(\sum_{a,u,v}P_{t,a}(u,v)z_{a,u,v}\right)^{\kappa_{q,t}}             \tag{11}
\]
sums the product probabilities over all assignments of local observation triples to the clusters represented by \(\kappa\).  The coefficient of \(z^{\omega_q}\) retains exactly those allocations having observation histogram \(\omega_q\).  If its label margins are \((n_{q,a})_a\), there are
\(
 \binom{m_q}{(n_{q,a})_a}
\)
equally likely allocations of those labels.  Division by this number and multiplication over cluster sizes proves
\[
 \Pr\{\omega\mid\kappa,n\}=H_{\kappa n\omega}.                            \tag{12}
\]
For incompatible margins the probability is zero.  Substituting every \(z_{a,u,v}=1\) in (11) shows that the compatible coefficients sum to the multinomial denominator, and hence
\[
 H_{\kappa n\omega}\ge0,\; \sum_{\omega}H_{\kappa n\omega}=1.           \tag{13}
\]
The argument remains valid at \(r_{q,a}=0,q\): the unique subset has probability one and (10) merely has a singleton range in one coordinate.  A label-constant treated-count menu likewise creates no division by zero.  Since the local denominators are positive integers and \(c\) is rational, (11)--(13) also prove that both \(H\) and \(\theta\) are rational.

As an independent smallest heterogeneous stress test, take sizes \((3,3,4)\), counts \((r_{3,1},r_{3,2})=(1,2)\), \((r_{4,1},r_{4,2})=(1,3)\), size-three response types \((0,1,3)\), \((2,12,15)\), and size-four response type \((0,1,6,15)\), where an integer records the low-to-high response bits in order \((1,1),(0,1),(1,2),(0,2)\).  Direct labeled enumeration over every label allocation and every feasible subset agrees cell by cell with (11)--(12) for all six assignment histograms.  In lexicographic order of the two label-one counts \((n_{3,1},n_{4,1})\), their support sizes are \(6,8,27,36,24,32\), and each of the six rational rows sums exactly to one.  This check uses the full observation histograms, not pairwise conflicts.

Write \(d_n\) for invariant design mass, \(\delta_{n\omega}\in[-L,L]\), and \(t_{n\omega}=d_n\delta_{n\omega}\).  By (12), the risk against response orbit \(\kappa\) is
\[
 r_\kappa(d,t)=\sum_{n,\omega}H_{\kappa n\omega}
       {\bigl(t_{n\omega}-d_n\theta_\kappa\bigr)^2\over d_n}.             \tag{14}
\]
At \(d_n=0\), the bounds \(|t_{n\omega}|\le Ld_n\) force \(t_{n\omega}=0\), and the closed perspective in (14) is zero.  Indeed, writing \(t=d\delta\) shows that each summand is \(dH(\delta-\theta)^2\), which converges uniformly to zero as \(d\downarrow0\).  Thus (14) is a continuous convex function on the compact set
\[
 \mathcal C=\{(d,t):d\ge0,\ \sum_nd_n=1,\ |t_{n\omega}|\le Ld_n\}.         \tag{15}
\]
Minimizing \(\max_\kappa r_\kappa\) over (15) is exactly \(\mathsf P\), so its value is attained.

For \(\pi\in\Delta(\mathcal K)\), apply the cited compact minimax theorem \(\texttt{lem:sion-compact-minimax}\) to
\[
 F((d,t),\pi)=\sum_\kappa\pi_\kappa r_\kappa(d,t)                         \tag{16}
\]
on the two compact convex sets (15) and \(\Delta(\mathcal K)\).  By (14), (16) is continuous and convex in \((d,t)\), and it is linear, hence concave, in \(\pi\).  The theorem gives
\[
 \min_{(d,t)\in\mathcal C}\max_\kappa r_\kappa(d,t)
 =\max_{\pi\in\Delta(\mathcal K)}\min_{(d,t)\in\mathcal C}F((d,t),\pi). \tag{17}
\]
For fixed \(\pi,n,\omega\), completing the square gives
\[
 \sum_\kappa\pi_\kappa H_{\kappa n\omega}
       (\delta-\theta_\kappa)^2
 =a_{n\omega}\left(\delta-{h_{n\omega}\over a_{n\omega}}\right)^2
  +\sum_\kappa\pi_\kappa H_{\kappa n\omega}\theta_\kappa^2
  -{h_{n\omega}^2\over a_{n\omega}}                                      \tag{18}
\]
when \(a_{n\omega}>0\).  The ratio \(h/a\) is a convex combination of values in \([-L,L]\), so it is feasible.  When \(a_{n\omega}=0\), nonnegativity implies every \(\pi_\kappa H_{\kappa n\omega}=0\), hence also \(h_{n\omega}=0\), and the whole cell contributes zero for every clipped decision.  Summing (18) over \(\omega\), then minimizing over \(d\), yields
\[
 \min_{(d,t)\in\mathcal C}F((d,t),\pi)=\min_{n\in\mathcal N}b_n(\pi).     \tag{19}
\]
Equations (17)--(19) are exactly \(\operatorname{val}(\mathsf P)=\operatorname{val}(\mathsf Q)=R^\star\).  Compactness and continuity give attainment on both sides.  Equation (18) supplies the posterior-mean rule on every positive-mass cell and proves that every value in \([-L,L]\) is valid on a zero-mass cell.

Finally, the three orbit counts are
\[
 \prod_{q=3}^b\binom{m_q+B_q-1}{B_q-1},\;
 \prod_{q=3}^b\binom{m_q+K-1}{K-1},\;
 \prod_{q=3}^b\binom{m_q+O_q-1}{O_q-1}.                                   \tag{20}
\]
The elementary bounds \(B_q\le h_0^q\le2^{2Kb}\), \(O_q\le K2^q\le K2^b\), and \(m_q\le m\), with fixed \(K,b\), turn the product of (20) and its kernel indices into
\(
 (m+1)^{O(2^{2Kb}+K2^b)}
\)
entries.  To implement an optimal \(d\), draw \(n\), allocate its labels uniformly to equal-size labeled clusters, and draw the exact-count subsets independently and uniformly.  Equation (12) proves that this realizes the optimized orbit experiment, and \(\texttt{lem:conditional-uniformity}\) proves that no nonuniform second-stage law can improve it.

For \(p\in\Delta(\mathcal A)\), conditional independence and the multinomial formula give exactly
\[
 d_n(p)=\prod_{q=3}^b\binom{m_q}{(n_{q,a})_{a\in\mathcal A}}
                    \prod_{a\in\mathcal A}p_a^{n_{q,a}},                  \tag{31}
\]
with \(0^0=1\).  The endpoint and orbit reductions in \(\texttt{thm:endpoint-orbit-equivalence}\) therefore identify the restricted minimax value as the minimum, over \(p\) and clipped tables \(\delta\), of the maximum over \(\kappa\) of the first family of expressions in \(\texttt{def:independence-feasibility-system}\).  This minimum is attained because the simplex and the finite decision cube are compact and the risks in (31) are continuous, including on the boundary.

Suppose first that \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}=R^\star=v\).  Choose an attaining restricted pair \((p,\delta)\).  By strong minimax duality in \(\texttt{thm:endpoint-orbit-equivalence}\), choose an attaining prior \(\pi\) with
\[
 \min_n b_n(\pi)=R^\star=v.                                                \tag{32}
\]
Optimality of \((p,\delta)\) gives a risk at most \(v\) against every \(\kappa\), and (32) gives \(b_n(\pi)\ge v\) for every \(n\).  Thus the finite system is feasible.

Conversely, suppose \((p,\delta,\pi,v)\) is feasible.  Its first inequalities and (31) imply \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}\le v\).  Its second inequalities and the dual formula imply \(R^\star\ge v\).  Since unrestricted designs contain the independent class, always \(R^\star\le R_{\mathrm{ind}}\).  Hence
\[
 R^\star=R_{\mathrm{ind}}=v,                                               \tag{33}
\]
which proves the equivalence.

It remains to prove the asserted equality conditions for every feasible solution, not merely for an optimizer selected afterward.  Put \(a_{n\omega}=a_{n\omega}(\pi)\) and \(h_{n\omega}=h_{n\omega}(\pi)\).  Averaging the first feasibility inequalities with weights \(\pi_\kappa\), and completing the square cell by cell, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v&\ge \sum_n d_n(p)\left[
 b_n(\pi)+\sum_{\omega:a_{n\omega}>0}
 a_{n\omega}\left(\delta_{n\omega}-{h_{n\omega}\over a_{n\omega}}\right)^2
 \right]                                                                  \\
 &\ge \sum_n d_n(p)b_n(\pi)\ge v.
\end{aligned}                                                               \tag{34}
\]
The middle inequality uses nonnegativity of squares, and the last uses \(b_n(\pi)\ge v\) and \(\sum_nd_n(p)=1\).  All inequalities in (34) are equalities.  Therefore, whenever \(d_n(p)>0\), one has \(b_n(\pi)=v\); and whenever also \(a_{n\omega}>0\), the corresponding square vanishes and
\(
 \delta_{n\omega}=h_{n\omega}/a_{n\omega}.
\)
If \(a_{n\omega}=0\), every \(\pi_\kappa H_{\kappa n\omega}=0\), so that cell contributes zero and any clipped value is permissible.  This proves all stated boundary assertions.

All quantities in this proof are rational and are evaluated using the orbit kernel already proved in \(\texttt{thm:endpoint-orbit-equivalence}\).  We display enough data to reproduce the certificate.

Encode a unit's four binary responses in the order \((1,1),(0,1),(1,2),(0,2)\) as the four low-to-high bits of an integer in \(\{0,\ldots,15\}\).  A size-three cluster type is a nondecreasing triple of these integers.  There are
\[
 T=\binom{16+3-1}{3}=816
\]
cluster types and \(\binom{816+1}{2}=333336\) two-cluster response orbits.  At label one, index a local outcome by \(k=3u+v\); at label two, index it by \(k=2u+v\).  Both indices range from zero to five.  The assignment orbits \(11,12,22\) consequently have \(21,36,21\) observation orbits, for a total of \(78\).

For a cluster type \(t\), let \(C_{a,t,k}\) be the number, among the three feasible exact-count subsets at label \(a\), that produce local index \(k\).  Thus \(P_{t,a}(k)=C_{a,t,k}/3\).  For an unordered pair \(\{t,t'\}\), define the integer likelihood row \(M_{tt',j}\), \(0\le j<78\), by
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 M_{tt',\{k,l\}_{11}}=2\{C_{1,t,k}C_{1,t',l}+\mathbf1_{k<l}C_{1,t,l}C_{1,t',k}\},& k\le l,\\
 M_{tt',(k,l)_{12}}=C_{1,t,k}C_{2,t',l}+C_{1,t',k}C_{2,t,l},&0\le k,l<6,\\
 M_{tt',\{k,l\}_{22}}=2\{C_{2,t,k}C_{2,t',l}+\mathbf1_{k<l}C_{2,t,l}C_{2,t',k}\},& k\le l.
\end{array}                                                               \tag{35}
\]
For each assignment block, the entries in (35) sum to \(18\), and \(M_{tt',j}/18\) is exactly the corresponding orbit likelihood.  Formula (35) is the specialization of the coefficient identity (12), including the two equally likely cluster-label orientations in orbit \(12\).

Use design masses
\[
 (q_{11},q_{12},q_{22})={1\over10^8}(50372138,42844038,6783824),             \tag{36}
\]
and, in the order upper-triangular \(11\), rectangular \(12\), upper-triangular \(22\), use endpoint decisions \(d_j=e_j/10^5\), where
\[
\begin{split}
(e_j)_{j=0}^{77}={}&(-78795,-99673,-125925,42873,13619,-28110,-131707,-161503,
21409,0,-22496,-189980,0,-21409,-43058,189980,161503,123041,131707,100384,81531,\\
&47551,0,-31307,-33852,-14286,-109350,21499,-22463,-30459,-80795,-69654,-145451,5723,
-93539,-52330,-155278,-89207,-178491,178491,71330,171200,14818,67123,-5722,\\
&145451,90301,68712,21192,47169,-21499,134172,-16612,102456,-11008,6753,-51501,
165520,114346,101636,42573,20700,0,65736,36413,50311,0,-93454,-33333,-33333,\\
&33333,-62461,1415,-49421,-150652,0,9511,-165520).
\end{split}                                                               \tag{37}
\]
Every entry in (37) lies in \([-3\cdot10^5,3\cdot10^5]\), so the rule is clipped.  If \(T(t)=\sum_{i,z,a}c_{z,a}Y_i(z,a)\), then the target for \(\{t,t'\}\) is \((T(t)+T(t'))/6\), and \(-18\le T(t)+T(t')\le18\).

For an integer target numerator \(h\in[-18,18]\) and cell \(j\), with \(g(j)\in\{11,12,22\}\), put
\[
 A_{h,j}=\left\lceil
 {q_{g(j)}(6e_j-10^5h)^2\,10^9\over(6\cdot10^5)^2}
 \right\rceil.                                                            \tag{38}
\]
Here the \(q\)'s in (38) are the rational probabilities in (36).  Summing (38) with the exact subset and orientation multiplicities in (35), over each of the \(333336\) response orbits, gives
\[
 \max_{t\le t'}{1\over18\cdot10^9}
 \sum_{j=0}^{77}M_{tt',j}A_{T(t)+T(t'),j}
 ={682490711\over500000000}.                                               \tag{39}
\]
Because each ceiling in (38) is outward, (39) proves the rigorous upper bound
\[
 R^\star\le {682490711\over500000000}=1.364981422.                          \tag{40}
\]
Equation (39) is an exhaustive integer check: the cluster types are the lexicographic triples \(0\le j_1\le j_2\le j_3\le15\), the response pairs are their upper triangle, and (35), (38) use only integer addition, multiplication, division with remainder, and a maximum.

\end{aligned}                                                               \tag{47}
\]
The Bayes lower bound in (47) holds for every nonlinear estimator and every \(p\), including \(p=0,1\).  Hence \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}>1.3659\).  Combining this with (40) proves
\[
 R_{\mathrm{ind}}-R^\star>1.3659-1.364981422=0.000918578.                  \tag{48}
\]

Finally let \(\tau_t\) be the target after replacing the contrast by \((3+t,-1-t,-1,-1)\).  For every schedule,
\[
 |\tau_t(Y)-\tau_0(Y)|
 =\left|{t\over6}\sum_{g,i}\{Y_{gi}(1,1)-Y_{gi}(0,1)\}\right|
 \le |t|.                                                                  \tag{49}
\]
For either design class, Minkowski's inequality applied before the supremum over \(Y\), followed by infimization over procedures, gives
\[
 \left|\sqrt{R_t}-\sqrt{R_0}\right|\le|t|.                                \tag{50}
\]
One may take a common unrestricted estimator space in (50), since projection onto the target interval cannot increase squared error.  The constant-zero rule and \(|\tau_0|\le3\) give \(\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{ind},0}},\sqrt{R^star_0}\le3\).  Therefore (48)--(50) imply
\[
 R_{\mathrm{ind},t}-R^star_t
 >0.000918578-2|t|
   \{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{ind},0}}+\sqrt{R^star_0}\}
 \ge0.000918578-12|t|>0.0007                                               \tag{51}
\]
whenever \(|t|\le10^{-5}\).  Rational \(t\) preserves the rational contrast and its zero coefficient sum, completing the claimed infinite rational neighborhood.

For one size-three cluster, let \(\rho\) send a local assignment \((a,S)\) to
\[
 \rho(a,S)=(3-a,S^c).                                                       \tag{52}
\]
Because \(r_{3,1}=1\) and \(r_{3,2}=2\), (52) is feasible and exchanges the two label classes.  Combine \(\rho\) with the coordinate map on schedules
\[
 (z,a)\longmapsto(1-z,3-a).                                                \tag{53}
\]
The four coefficients satisfy
\[
 c_{1,1}=c_{0,2}=1,\; c_{0,1}=c_{1,2}=-1,                                  \tag{54}
\]
so (53) preserves the target.  It also preserves the bounded anonymous-saturation model and maps the observation under (52) bijectively to the old observation.  Unit permutations act transitively on the three subsets within either label, while (52) connects the two labels.  Hence the group generated by unit permutations and \(\rho\) is transitive on all six local assignments.

Apply an independent uniform element of this six-point transitive action in every cluster to an arbitrary design and transform its rule as in the conditional-Jensen construction of \(\texttt{lem:conditional-uniformity}\).  Equations (53)--(54) replace equation (1) in that argument, so worst-case risk does not increase.  The product action is transitive on the Cartesian product of the local assignment spaces.  Averaging any law over it therefore gives the uniform law on all \(6^m\) global assignments.  This is exactly independent cluster labels with common probability \(1/2\), followed by independent uniform selection of a size-one subset at label one and its size-two analogue at label two.

Thus every unrestricted procedure has an independent-common-probability symmetrization with no greater maximum risk, which gives \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}\le R^\star\).  The reverse inequality follows because the independent class is a subclass of unrestricted designs.  Consequently \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}=R^\star\) for every \(m\), and the common probability \(1/2\) is minimax.  This also supplies a feasible equality point in the characterization of \(\texttt{thm:independence-frontier}\).

theorem.statement: For every fixed \(K\) and \(b\), the handle \(\mathfrak C\) can be implemented in the Turing model as follows.  On every rational feasible treated-count table \(0\le r_{q,a}\le q\), including boundary entries and menus constant in \(a\), every rational contrast \(c\), every size profile \(s\), and every rational \(\varepsilon>0\), it constructs the exact rational orbit kernel \(H\), weakly optimizes \(\mathsf P\) and \(\mathsf Q\), and, in time polynomial in the displayed orbit-program size, the rational input bit length, and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\), returns a rational implementable design, a rational endpoint estimator table, and a rational \(\varepsilon\)-least-favorable prior.  Direct rational evaluation produces \(\underline R\le R^\star\le\overline R\) with \(\overline R-\underline R\le\varepsilon\).  It also returns a division-free Bernoulli-histogram recursion defining the continuous-outcome estimator on every observation, including all zero-design-mass and zero-prior-likelihood faces.  This is weak approximation only and does not assert rational exact optimizers.
theorem.proof_tex:
Let \(J=|\mathcal N|\), \(E=|\mathcal K|\), and let \(W\) denote the number of compatible \((n,\omega)\) cells.  These dimensions are part of the displayed orbit-program size.  Let \(B\) be the maximum input bit length.

We first construct the kernel.  For fixed \(K,b\), enumerate the \(2^{2K}\) unit-response words, their size-\(q\) multisets, the response histograms, label histograms, and observation histograms in lexicographic order.  The numerator in each local probability \(P_{t,a}(u,v)\) is obtained by at most \(2^b\) subset tests, and its denominator is the positive integer \(\binom q{r_{q,a}}\), including the value one at boundary counts.  To compute a coefficient in \(F_{\kappa,q}\), multiply its local factors one cluster at a time and retain a table indexed by observation-count vectors of total degree at most \(m_q\).  There are at most \((m_q+1)^{O_q}\) states and at most \(O_q\) transitions per state.  The denominator after at most \(m_q\) multiplications divides a product of \(m_q\) fixed local denominators; the final multinomial divisor has at most \(O(m_q\log m_q)\) bits.  Thus every intermediate numerator and denominator has \(O(B+m\log m)\) bits, and the complete table \(H\), together with the rational values \(\theta_\kappa\), is produced by a number of bit operations polynomial in its displayed output size and \(B\).  The normalization proof (13) detects any incompatible margin and supplies an exact row-sum check.

We next give a bit-safe weak-optimization reduction that does not require the original conic program to satisfy Slater's condition.  On the compact perspective set (15), put
\[
 F_{\rm pr}(d,t)=\max_{\kappa\in\mathcal K}r_\kappa(d,t).                   \tag{21}
\]
Let \(\varepsilon_0=\min\{\varepsilon,1\}\), choose a rational
\[
 0<\lambda\le
 \min\left\{{1\over4},{\varepsilon_0\over64\max\{1,L^2\}}\right\},
 \; \eta={\lambda\over J}.                                                \tag{22}
\]
The bit length of (22) is polynomial in \(B+\log J+\log(1/\varepsilon)\).  Mix any procedure with weight \(\lambda\) with the uniform distribution on assignment orbits using decision zero.  Since \(\theta_\kappa^2\le L^2\), convexity of the perspectives proves that the resulting point has every \(d_n\ge\eta\) and risk at most
\[
 (1-\lambda)F_{\rm pr}(d,t)+\lambda L^2.                                  \tag{23}
\]
Consequently restricting to \(d_n\ge\eta\) raises the optimum by at most \(\lambda L^2\).

On \(d_n\ge\eta\), every rational value of (21) is computed exactly in polynomial bit time.  Moreover, for a summand of (14),
\[
 \left|{\partial r_\kappa\over\partial t_{n\omega}}\right|
   =2H_{\kappa n\omega}\left|{t_{n\omega}\over d_n}-\theta_\kappa\right|
   \le4LH_{\kappa n\omega},
\]
and
\[
 \left|{\partial r_\kappa\over\partial d_n}\right|
 =\left|\sum_\omega H_{\kappa n\omega}
       \left(\theta_\kappa^2-{t_{n\omega}^2\over d_n^2}\right)\right|
 \le L^2.                                                                  \tag{24}
\]
Thus an explicit Lipschitz constant for (21), polynomially encoded in \(J,W,L\), follows from (24).  After eliminating one simplex coordinate, the constraints \(d_n\ge\eta\) and \(|t_{n\omega}|\le Ld_n\) form a rational convex body with an explicit outer ball and, after replacing \(\eta\) by a constant multiple of \(\eta\), an explicit inner ball of radius at least \(2^{-\operatorname{poly}(B+\log J+\log(1/\varepsilon))}\).  Membership is decided by rational linear inequalities and (21) has an exact rational value oracle.

Apply \(\texttt{lem:weak-rational-convex-optimization}\) to nested versions of this body.  The inner version supplies the erosion required by the cited theorem; (23)--(24) bound the loss from moving the optimum to that erosion.  Ask for geometric and value errors small enough that their sum under the Lipschitz bound is at most \(\varepsilon_0/8\).  The theorem returns a rational near-feasible point in time polynomial in the stated quantities.  Exact feasibility is recovered by projecting its \(d\)-coordinates onto the lower-bounded simplex and clipping each \(t_{n\omega}\) to \([-Ld_n,Ld_n]\).  Projection onto a rational lower-bounded simplex is computed by sorting the rational coordinates and subtracting the rational threshold on the active set, so the repaired point is rational and polynomial-time computable.  The distance and (24) bounds show that its directly evaluated value \(\overline R\) satisfies
\[
 R^\star\le\overline R\le R^\star+{\varepsilon_0\over4}.                 \tag{25}
\]
Here division is only by the strictly positive repaired \(d_n\), so zero faces have not been used as a numerical regularity assumption.

For the lower certificate define
\[
 G(\pi)=\min_{n\in\mathcal N}b_n(\pi).                                    \tag{26}
\]
For fixed \(n\), completing the square as in (18) evaluates \(b_n(\pi)\) exactly at every rational \(\pi\): when \(a_{n\omega}=0\), nonnegativity forces \(h_{n\omega}=0\) and the term is set to zero.  Equivalently,
\[
 b_n(\pi)=\min_{u\in[-L,L]^{\mathcal W_n}}
 \sum_\kappa\pi_\kappa\sum_\omega
 H_{\kappa n\omega}(u_\omega-\theta_\kappa)^2.                           \tag{27}
\]
Each loss vector in (27) lies in \([0,4L^2]^E\).  Taking an infimum and then a minimum therefore gives the global bound
\[
 |G(\pi)-G(\pi')|\le4L^2\|\pi-\pi'\|_1.                                  \tag{28}
\]
The function \(-G\) is convex: each \(b_n\) is an infimum of linear functions of \(\pi\), hence concave, and the minimum over \(n\) is concave by (27), since it is the Bayes risk when the decision maker may also choose \(n\).  Its rational value oracle evaluates all \(b_n\)'s by (18).  Apply the cited weak-optimization theorem on the rational simplex, use a nested simplex to handle its boundary, project the returned rational point exactly onto the simplex, and invoke (28).  At precision \(\varepsilon_0/4\) this gives rational \(\widehat\pi\) and the directly computed number
\[
 \underline R=G(\widehat\pi)\ge R^\star-{\varepsilon_0\over4},           \tag{29}
\]
where equality \(\max_\pi G(\pi)=R^\star\) is supplied by \(\texttt{thm:endpoint-orbit-equivalence}\).  Equations (25) and (29), with each internal tolerance halved if necessary, give \(\overline R-\underline R\le\varepsilon_0\le\varepsilon\).  Both bounds are checked after optimization by the finite rational formulas (14) and (18); hence a faulty numerical oracle cannot validate its own certificate.
Setting each dual epigraph coordinate to \(\rho_{n\omega}=h_{n\omega}^2/a_{n\omega}\) when \(a_{n\omega}>0\), and to zero otherwise, turns \((\widehat\pi,\underline R)\) into a rational feasible point of \(\mathsf Q\).  Likewise the repaired \((d,t,\overline R)\) is a rational feasible point of \(\mathsf P\).  Thus the two weak optimizations are represented in the advertised conic coordinates as well as by their directly evaluated risk forms.

Recover the rational endpoint decision by \(\delta_{n\omega}=t_{n\omega}/d_n\) on the positive design returned above, and set every formally unused cell to zero.  Likewise set the posterior decision to \(h/a\) for \(a>0\) and to zero for \(a=0\).  For arbitrary revealed \(v\in[0,1]^N\), the continuous rule is the finite polynomial
\[
 \overline\delta(x,v)=
 \sum_{e\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal O(x)}}
 \delta_{[x,e]}
 \prod_{j:e_j=1}v_j\prod_{j:e_j=0}(1-v_j).                                \tag{30}
\]
It has no division and is therefore total on every face.  To evaluate (30) without enumerating \(2^N\) outcomes, first convolve the Bernoulli factors within each bounded cluster to obtain the distribution of its \((a,u,v)\) triple, then convolve those local distributions into size-tagged observation histograms and take the dot product with the endpoint table.  The state spaces are the same bounded-alphabet histogram spaces used to construct \(H\), so this returns the promised decoder in polynomial output time.  This completes the Turing-model construction, while making no assertion that an exact optimizer has rational coordinates.

added_lemmas.statement: Let \(M\) and \(N\) be compact convex subsets of linear topological spaces.  If a real function on \(M\times N\) is upper semicontinuous and quasi-concave in its first argument and lower semicontinuous and quasi-convex in its second argument, then its max--min equals its min--max.  In particular, the equality applies to a continuous function that is affine in one argument and convex in the other, after interchanging signs and arguments as needed.

source.verbatim_statement: Let \(M\) and \(N\) be convex, compact spaces, and \(f\) a function on \(M\times N\), quasi-concave-convex and u.s.c.-l.s.c. Then \(\sup\inf f=\inf\sup f\).

attestation.note: Transcribed from Maurice Sion, On general minimax theorems, Pacific Journal of Mathematics 8 (1958), Theorem 3.4, publisher PDF.

added_lemmas.statement: For a finite-dimensional convex body supplied with rationally encoded inner and outer radius bounds, polynomial-time weak membership and rational approximate-value oracles permit weak constrained convex-function minimization in oracle-polynomial time.  The output accuracy enters the running time through its logarithm; the returned point and value may be chosen rational.

proposed.statement: For fixed \(K\) and \(b\), every rational table satisfying \(0\le r_{q,a}\le q\), including tables with boundary entries or a treated-count menu constant in \(a\), every rational contrast \(c\), and every size profile \(s\), \(R^\star\) is unchanged when nature is restricted to binary schedules. Every endpoint estimator table \(d\) has the multilinear extension \(\overline d\) from \(\texttt{def:endpoint-extension}\) with \(\sup_{Y\in\mathcal M}\mathcal R(D,\overline d;Y)\le\max_{Y\in\mathcal M\cap\{0,1\}^{2KN}}\mathcal R(D,d;Y)\). Moreover, invariant procedures and priors reduce the unrestricted game exactly to \(\operatorname{val}(\mathsf P)=\operatorname{val}(\mathsf Q)=R^\star\), with rational kernel \(H\), attainment, a posterior-mean endpoint rule on positive-mass cells, arbitrary clipped values on zero-mass cells, and an implementable correlated design obtained from assignment histograms followed by the conditional uniform sampling of \(\texttt{lem:conditional-uniformity}\). The orbit data have at most \((m+1)^{O(2^{2Kb}+K2^b)}\) entries.
proposed.justification: This is the lossless finite reduction for every feasible exact-count menu, including pure-control, pure-treatment, and label-constant menus, while retaining the full observation hypergraph.
proposed.gap: SudijonoDobribanTchetgenTchetgen2026 and Hull2026 obtain endpoint reductions for no interference, while KandirosHarshawSavje2026 bounds a graph-indexed network game; none gives an exact polynomial-size orbit game for a non-pairwise exact-count observation hypergraph.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix the asserted size-three cluster \(g\), and abbreviate its three label-one control-exposure coordinates by
\[
 e_i=(g,i,0,1),\qquad i\in\{1,2,3\}.
\]
Call a set \(T\) of potential-outcome coordinates jointly observable when there is an \(X\in\mathcal X\) such that \(T\subseteq\mathcal O(X)\).  This is only shorthand for the declared observation map, not an additional assumption.  Since \(K=2\), label \(1\) belongs to \(\mathcal A\).  The hypothesis \(r_{3,1}=1\), which is compatible with \(\texttt{ass:interior-exact-counts}\), and the definition of the feasible assignment space give
\[
 A_g=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 S_g\in\bigl\{\{1\},\{2\},\{3\}\bigr\}.
\]
Indeed, feasibility requires \(S_g\subseteq\{1,2,3\}\) and \(|S_g|=r_{3,1}=1\), and these are exactly the three singleton subsets.

For \(k\in\{1,2,3\}\), take \(A_g=1\) and \(S_g=\{k\}\).  By the definition of \(\mathcal O\), the part of the resulting observation hyperedge belonging to cluster \(g\) is
\[
 \mathcal O_g(k)
 =\{(g,k,1,1)\}\mathbin{\cup}\{e_i:i\in\{1,2,3\}\setminus\{k\}\}.
\]
The complete enumeration is therefore
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
k&\mathcal O_g(k)\cap\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}\\ \hline
1&\{e_2,e_3\}\\
2&\{e_1,e_3\}\\
3&\{e_1,e_2\}.
\end{array}
\]
Each local choice extends to an element of \(\mathcal X\): for every other cluster \(h\), choose any \(a_h\in\mathcal A\) and then a subset of \(\{1,\ldots,s_h\}\) of cardinality \(r_{s_h,a_h}\); such a subset exists because the declared range of \(r\) gives \(0\le r_{s_h,a_h}\le s_h\).  Hence, for distinct \(i,j\), choosing \(k\) to be the remaining index produces a feasible \(X\) for which
\[
 \{e_i,e_j\}\subseteq\mathcal O(X).
\]
Thus every pair is jointly observable.

Conversely, suppose that all three coordinates were jointly observable.  Then some \(X\in\mathcal X\) would satisfy \(e_i\in\mathcal O(X)\) for every \(i\).  The definition of \(\mathcal O(X)\) first forces \(A_g=1\), because the fourth component of every \(e_i\) is \(1\), and then forces
\[
 \mathbf 1\{i\in S_g\}=0\qquad(i=1,2,3).
\]
Consequently \(S_g=\varnothing\) and \(|S_g|=0\).  Feasibility at \(A_g=1\), however, requires
\[
 |S_g|=r_{3,1}=1,
\]
a contradiction.  Therefore \(\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}\) is not jointly observable.

For the graph conclusion, let
\[
 \mathfrak F=\{T:T\subseteq\mathcal O(X)\text{ for some }X\in\mathcal X\}
\]
be the compatibility family of the exact-count observation hypergraph.  If a simple pairwise conflict graph had independent sets exactly \(\mathfrak F\), then the joint observability of every pair \(\{e_i,e_j\}\) would imply that none of the three pairs is an edge.  By the definition of an independent set, \(\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}\) would then be independent and hence would belong to \(\mathfrak F\), contradicting the preceding paragraph.  Thus no such graph representation exists.

Finally, the failure is not erased by the orbit construction.  For any binary size-three response type \(t\), \(\texttt{def:local-kernel}\), \(\binom31=3\), and \(r_{3,1}=1\) give the exact identity
\[
 P_{t,1}(u,v)
 =\frac13\sum_{k=1}^{3}
 \mathbf 1\!\left\{
 t_{k,1,1}=u,\ \sum_{i\ne k}t_{i,0,1}=v
 \right\}.
\]
Every summand is generated by precisely the local hyperedge \(\mathcal O_g(k)\); there is no summand corresponding to \(S_g=\varnothing\), which would be necessary to reveal \(e_1,e_2,e_3\) together.  In \(\texttt{def:orbit-kernel}\), \(F_{\kappa,3}(z)\) is a product of sums having these nonnegative \(P_{t,a}(u,v)\) as coefficients.  Coefficient extraction therefore aggregates only products of feasible local exact-count observations and cannot create support absent from every local factor.  For compatible label margins the normalizing multinomial coefficient is a positive integer, while incompatible margins are assigned coefficient zero by definition.  Thus passage from labeled observations to \(H_{\kappa n\omega}\) may identify the three singleton choices under symmetry, but it neither introduces an empty treated subset nor assigns positive mass to the forbidden three-control observation.  Hence \(H\) retains exactly the triple obstruction established above.
